## Domain review — deviations from intended interventions

| Signalling question | Proposed answer | Warrant and uncertainty |
|---|---|---|
| **2.1 Participants aware** | **Probably yes (retain)** | The report calls the study observer-blinded and specifies that the examining physician did not know assignment; it does not say participants were blinded (primary source, p. 2, lines 121–127; p. 4, lines 13–21). A conspicuous 39-hour-per-week, three-week treatment program versus no treatment makes participant awareness probable (p. 4, lines 36–48; 104–109), but this is indirect rather than direct evidence. Retain the uncertainty that participant knowledge is not expressly reported. |
| **2.2 Carers/delivery personnel aware** | **Probably yes (retain)** | The intensive program was delivered by staff, unlike the untreated control condition (p. 4, lines 36–48, 90–103, 104–109). This supports probable provider awareness, but the report identifies blinding only for the examining physician (p. 4, lines 13–21) and does not directly establish which intervention personnel knew assignments. Retain this uncertainty. |
| **2.3 Trial-context deviations** | **No information (retain)** | Non-initiation and treatment dropout are reported, with reasons including not appearing, treatment being too difficult, and increased pain (p. 3, lines 101–104; p. 4, lines 4–12). Controls could seek treatment elsewhere (p. 4, lines 104–109). The source does not establish whether these departures or outside treatment were protocol-inconsistent, or whether trial context caused them. Under the supplied guidance, neither non-adherence nor outside treatment alone warrants a yes. |
| **2.6 Appropriate assignment-effect analysis** | **No (retain)** | The target is assignment among all randomized participants. The report randomized 106 people but excluded the two who never started and seven who dropped out; only two of those nine were contacted at four months, and the article says they were not included in the analysis (p. 3, lines 4–13; p. 6, lines 83–94). The workability result instead compares 45 treated and 49 control returnees (p. 5, lines 73–90). This is post-randomization exclusion of eligible randomized participants, not merely an appropriate modified-ITT exclusion for missing outcomes. The reported returnee comparison is not an all-randomized assignment estimate. Outcomes for the excluded participants are unknown. |
| **2.7 Potential substantial impact** | **Probably yes (retain, with qualification)** | The nine excluded participants are a modest share of 106, and workability was common among returnees; those facts temper the concern. But exclusions included noncompletion associated with difficulty accepting the program or increased pain, while participants’ workability outcomes are unknown (p. 4, lines 4–12; p. 6, lines 83–94). These reasons could be prognostically relevant to ability to work, so the exclusions could substantially affect the result; the direction and magnitude cannot be determined. |

The frozen draft’s main revisions are therefore unnecessary: its proposed answers are supportable under the supplied D2 guidance. The key qualification is to keep the 2.7 conclusion explicitly potential and uncertain, not to imply demonstrated bias.
